report:
## Research Findings

The current best evidence does **not** support the claim that saw palmetto improves BPH symptoms over placebo in the longer term — in fact, the weight of high-quality trial evidence points the opposite way.

**Key evidence:**
- The 2006 NEJM STEP trial (225 men, 1 year, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found saw palmetto extract produced no significant improvement in urinary symptom scores, peak flow rate, prostate size, quality of life, or PSA compared with placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085).
- A follow-up NIH-sponsored trial testing escalating doses (up to triple-strength) over longer duration likewise found no dose-related benefit over placebo (referenced in https://urologyandmenshealth.com/saw-palmetto-bph-evidence-review/).
- The Cochrane systematic review (updated 2012, 32 RCTs, 5,666 men) concluded that even at double or triple standard doses, Serenoa repens provided no improvement in nocturia, peak urine flow, or symptom scores versus placebo (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001423.pub3/abstract).
- A 2023 update of this Cochrane review (Serenoa repens monotherapy) reaffirmed: "Serenoa repens alone provides little to no benefit for men with lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement," with moderate-to-high certainty evidence (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10286776/).

Earlier, smaller, often industry-associated or open-label trials (pre-2000s) had suggested modest benefit, but these were generally short-duration, poorly blinded, or used varying preparations — limitations addressed by later rigorous trials.

**Conclusion:** Contrary to the premise, robust long-term, placebo-controlled evidence (NEJM STEP trial and Cochrane systematic reviews) indicates saw palmetto does **not** meaningfully improve BPH symptoms compared with placebo. Some uncertainty remains regarding combination phytotherapy products, but monotherapy shows no consistent long-term benefit.
